passage:
Day one. Ms Ritu handed back Kalyani's essay with red ink on nearly every line. "Again," was all she said. Kalyani stuffed it into her bag, cheeks hot, thinking Ms Ritu enjoyed this.

Two weeks later. Fourth draft. Ms Ritu read it standing at the desk. "Now it says what you mean." It wasn't praise exactly, but Kalyani walked out taller than she'd walked in.

Six years later. In her first-year seminar, the professor read out Kalyani's paragraph as a model. That evening she visited her old school and found Ms Ritu in the staffroom. "Thank you for all that red ink," she said. Ms Ritu laughed, then grew serious. "I was too sharp with some of your classmates. It worked for you. It doesn't always." Kalyani nodded. She knew a friend who had stopped writing altogether.

qa.q: How many drafts did Kalyani write before Ms Ritu said "Now it says what you mean"?
What was Kalyani feeling on the first day when she stuffed her essay into her bag?
qa.a: Anger and hurt. Her cheeks were hot and she thought Ms Ritu enjoyed marking so harshly.

qa.q: What should Kalyani take from Ms Ritu's remark that being sharp worked for her but doesn't always?
qa.a: That harshness helping her once does not make it right for everyone. She can thank Ms Ritu while still seeing that some students, like her friend, may be hurt by it.

qa.q: How does Ms Ritu see her own teaching years later?
qa.a: With some doubt. She admits she was too sharp with some students, so she sees that what worked for Kalyani did not work for everyone.

grounding: Years later the protagonist thanks a hard teacher while recognising that harshness is not always good.

passage:
On his way back from the town college admission office, Lokesh stopped at the old primary school in Chandpur. Usha teacher was still there, grey now, marking copies under the neem tree.
She had been the strictest teacher in the village. She made him rewrite every sum until it was perfect. She'd once kept him back till dark over one wrong answer. He'd hated her for it.
Now he'd got into the science stream with the highest maths marks in the block.
"Teacher, I came to say thank you," he said, touching her feet. "You pushed me when I wanted to give up."
Usha teacher smiled, her eyes wet.
Walking home, Lokesh passed his little brother's school, where a teacher was shouting at a small boy and twisting his ear. Lokesh stopped. Usha teacher had been strict. She had never been cruel. That was different, and he'd make sure his brother knew it.

qa.q: Where was Usha teacher marking copies?
How did Lokesh feel about Usha teacher when he was younger?
qa.a: He resented her strictness and felt angry, especially at being kept back till dark over one wrong answer.

qa.q: What did Lokesh understand when he passed his brother's school?
qa.a: That strictness and cruelty are different, so harshness is not good just because Usha teacher's strictness helped him.

qa.q: How might Usha teacher feel when Lokesh thanks her?
qa.a: She seems deeply moved and proud, her eyes wet, to see her strictness had helped him.

grounding: A teen realises years later that a strict teacher pushed him well and thanks her, while recognising harshness is not always good.

passage:
Ada hadn't been back to her old music school in Osaka in three years. The corridor still smelled of floor wax and old sheet music.
Mr Kaito was in room 4, as always, correcting a small boy's hand position. He had been the strictest teacher she'd ever had. Scales for forty minutes. No pieces until her fingers were "honest." She had cried in the stairwell more than once.
Last month she'd won second place at the national youth competition, and everyone said her technique was clean.
When the boy left, Ada bowed. "Sensei, I came to thank you. The scales were terrible. And they worked."
Mr Kaito's face softened. "You worked," he said.
On the train home, Ada thought about her friend Hina's teacher, who threw pencils and called students hopeless. That wasn't the same as Mr Kaito at all. Hard could be good. Cruel never was.

qa.q: What place did Ada win at the national youth competition?
What was Ada feeling when she thanked Mr Kaito?
qa.a: She felt grateful and a little emotional, seeing that his strict scales had helped her succeed.

qa.q: What did Ada realise on the train home?
qa.a: That strict teaching like Mr Kaito's can help, but harshness like throwing pencils is cruel and not good just because hard work sometimes pays off.

qa.q: How does Mr Kaito respond to Ada's thanks?
qa.a: He seems touched and humble, giving credit to her own hard work.

grounding: A teen realises years later that a strict teacher pushed her well and thanks him, without assuming all harshness is good.
